startScreenOptions.shortStartDescription: Interactive lecture with 4 embedded questions for AN78.1-AN78.5.

interactions.label: Why does implantation at an ectopic site, such as the fallopian tube, pose a thr

params.question: Why does implantation at an ectopic site, such as the fallopian tube, pose a threat to the mother's life?

answers.text: The ectopic embryo suppresses maternal immunity, leaving the mother vulnerable to infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the trophoblast does modulate immunity, this is not why ectopic pregnancy is dangerous. The threat comes from invasive growth at a site not designed to support pregnancy.

answers.text: The ectopic blastocyst produces cytotoxins that damage surrounding maternal organs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The blastocyst does not produce cytotoxins. The danger lies in the continued invasive growth of the trophoblast at a site not equipped to contain it.

answers.text: The blastocyst continues to grow and invade tissue at a site that cannot safely support pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The trophoblast is inherently invasive — it will burrow into whatever tissue it contacts. In a thin-walled structure like the fallopian tube, this can lead to rupture and life-threatening haemorrhage.

answers.text: The mother's immune system mounts a hyperacute rejection response against the ectopic embryo

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ectopic pregnancy is not caused by immune rejection — the trophoblast actively evades immune responses. The danger is from its invasive growth at an abnormal site.

overallFeedback.feedback: An ectopically implanted blastocyst is dangerous because its trophoblast continues to invade surrounding tissue. In sites like the fallopian tube, this growth can cause rupture and life-threatening haemorrhage.
Exactly. The trophoblast will invade whatever tissue it contacts, regardless of location. In ectopic sites like the fallopian tube, this invasive growth can threaten the mother's life.

interactions.label: The syncytiotrophoblast expands during implantation by undergoing its own mitoti

params.question: The syncytiotrophoblast expands during implantation by undergoing its own mitotic divisions.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. The syncytiotrophoblast has no cell boundaries — it is a single fused multinucleated mass and cannot divide. It grows exclusively by incorporating cells from the cytotrophoblast, which divides and feeds cells outward. This divide → fuse → invade relationship is a key distinction.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: That's right — the syncytiotrophoblast is a continuous multinucleated mass that cannot undergo mitosis. It grows only by absorbing new cells from the underlying cytotrophoblast, which is the actively dividing layer.

interactions.label: When the extraembryonic mesoderm splits into two layers, what structure is forme

params.question: When the extraembryonic mesoderm splits into two layers, what structure is formed by the outer layer together with the overlying trophoblast?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The outer (somatic) layer of extraembryonic mesoderm lines the trophoblast, and together they form the chorion — the outermost fetal membrane that will contribute to the placenta.
The yolk sac wall is formed by the inner (splanchnic) layer of extraembryonic mesoderm combined with the endodermal lining of the yolk sac — not the outer layer.
The connecting stalk is the bridge of tissue that survives when the extraembryonic coelom splits the mesoderm. It does not form from the outer layer plus trophoblast.
The outer layer of extraembryonic mesoderm covers the amnion, but the amnion is a separate structure. The combination of this layer with the trophoblast specifically forms the chorion.

overallFeedback.feedback: When the extraembryonic coelom splits the mesoderm, its outer (somatic) layer combines with the trophoblast to form the chorion. The inner (splanchnic) layer combines with the yolk sac lining to form the yolk sac wall.
Well done. The chorion — formed by the somatic extraembryonic mesoderm plus the trophoblast — is the outermost fetal membrane and the precursor to the fetal side of the placenta.

interactions.label: During the second week, embryonic nutrition transitions between two modes. Which

params.question: During the second week, embryonic nutrition transitions between two modes. Which of the following correctly describes this shift?

answers.text: Nutrition from the yolk sac's stored lipid reserves is followed by haemotrophic nutrition from maternal blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The human yolk sac does not provide significant lipid-based nutrition. Early embryonic nutrition comes from endometrial gland secretions (histotrophic), not from yolk reserves.

answers.text: Haemotrophic nutrition from maternal blood is replaced by histotrophic nutrition from gland secretions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sequence is reversed. Histotrophic nutrition comes first, when the embryo relies on endometrial gland secretions. Haemotrophic nutrition follows as the trophoblast invades maternal blood vessels.

answers.text: Nutrition from the mature placenta is followed by histotrophic nutrition from decidual cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mature placenta forms much later in development. During the second week, the sequence is histotrophic (gland secretions) followed by haemotrophic (direct maternal blood contact).

answers.text: Histotrophic nutrition from uterine gland secretions is followed by haemotrophic nutrition from maternal blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Initially the embryo is nourished by secretions from endometrial glands (histotrophic). As the syncytiotrophoblast erodes into maternal sinusoids, nutrition shifts to direct exchange with maternal blood (haemotrophic).

overallFeedback.feedback: During the second week, the embryo first feeds on endometrial gland secretions (histotrophic nutrition). As the trophoblast invades maternal blood vessels, nutrition becomes haemotrophic — derived directly from maternal blood.
Exactly. The histotrophic-to-haemotrophic shift is one of the defining 'twos' of the second week and is key to understanding early placental physiology.
